name: Greco-Roman religion
summary: The polytheistic religion of the Greek and Roman worlds centred on sacrifice, festivals, oracles and civic cults rather than a single sacred book. Poets such as Homer and Hesiod gave the gods their stories, while mystery cults such as those of Eleusis, Isis and Mithras offered personal initiation. Its temples, myths and ideas about the divine passed into later Western culture even after Christianity displaced it.

name: Ancient Israel & the Hebrew Bible
summary: The kingdoms of Israel and Judah and the exile in Babylon form the setting in which the books of the Hebrew Bible were composed, edited and collected. Tradition ascribes the Torah to Moses and the Psalms to David; most modern scholars see the texts as the work of many hands over centuries, taking much of their final shape during and after the Babylonian exile. The result became the scripture of Judaism and the Old Testament of Christianity.

name: Second Temple Judaism
summary: Between the rebuilding of the Jerusalem Temple and its destruction by Rome, Judaism was diverse: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and others debated law, purity and the end of days. The period produced the Greek Septuagint, apocalyptic writings, the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Hellenistic Jewish philosophy of Philo. Both Rabbinic Judaism and Christianity grew out of it.

name: Early Christianity & the New Testament
summary: Followers of Jesus of Nazareth spread their movement from Judea across the Roman Empire, at first as a Jewish sect and increasingly among gentiles. Paul's letters and the four Gospels, written in Greek within roughly a century of Jesus's death, were gathered with other texts into the New Testament. Christians faced periodic persecution until Constantine's toleration in 313.

name: Church Fathers & the Councils
summary: Theologians writing in Greek, Latin and Syriac defined Christian doctrine, interpreted scripture and argued against rivals they considered heretical. The ecumenical councils from Nicaea (325) to Chalcedon (451) and beyond fixed the creeds on the Trinity and the nature of Christ. Origen, Athanasius, the Cappadocians, Jerome and Augustine shaped all later theology, East and West.

name: Rabbinic Judaism
summary: After the destruction of the Temple, the rabbis reorganised Jewish life around Torah study, prayer and law. Their oral teaching was codified in the Mishnah around 200 and expanded in the Jerusalem and Babylonian Talmuds, together with collections of scriptural interpretation called midrash. This rabbinic tradition became normative Judaism for the following millennium and a half.

name: Monasticism
summary: Christian ascetics withdrew first into the Egyptian and Syrian deserts and then into organised communities living under a rule of prayer, work and obedience. The Rule of St Benedict became the standard in the Latin West, and Irish and Anglo-Saxon monasteries became centres of learning and book production. Monasteries preserved texts, ran estates and sent out missionaries across Europe.

name: Byzantine Orthodoxy
summary: The Greek-speaking Christianity of the Eastern Roman Empire, centred on Constantinople, developed its own liturgy, iconography, mystical theology and church law. The iconoclast controversies of the 8th and 9th centuries ended with the restoration of icons, and missions carried Orthodoxy to the Slavs. Tensions with Rome culminated in the schism traditionally dated to 1054.

name: Medieval scholasticism & mysticism
summary: In cathedral schools and new universities, scholastics such as Anselm, Peter Lombard and Aquinas used logic and recovered Aristotle to systematise Christian doctrine. Alongside them a rich mystical literature, from Bernard and Hildegard to Eckhart, Julian of Norwich and the Devotio Moderna, explored the soul's direct experience of God, often in the vernacular.

name: Mendicant orders
summary: The Franciscans and Dominicans, founded in the early 13th century, combined vows of poverty with preaching in the growing towns. Francis of Assisi's ideal of evangelical poverty and Dominic's order of preachers produced many of the leading theologians of the universities, including Aquinas and Bonaventure. Debates over poverty and over the friars' privileges ran through the late Middle Ages.

name: Medieval Jewish thought
summary: Jewish scholars in the Islamic world, Spain, Provence and northern France produced biblical and talmudic commentary, legal codes, philosophy and poetry. Rashi's commentaries, Maimonides's code and philosophy, Judah Halevi's Kuzari and the Kabbalah of the Zohar became classics. This creativity unfolded amid periods of tolerance and of persecution, culminating in the expulsion from Spain in 1492.

name: Protestant Reformation
summary: Building on humanist scholarship and earlier reform movements, Luther, Zwingli, Calvin and others broke with the papacy and taught justification by faith and the authority of scripture. Printing spread vernacular Bibles, catechisms and hymns. The result was a lasting division of Western Christianity into Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Anabaptist churches alongside Roman Catholicism.

name: Catholic Reformation
summary: The Roman Catholic Church responded to Protestantism and to its own reform currents with the Council of Trent, new religious orders such as the Jesuits, and a flowering of mysticism in Spain. Historians debate whether to call it the Counter-Reformation, stressing reaction, or the Catholic Reformation, stressing renewal. It shaped Catholic worship, education and missions for four centuries.

name: Puritanism & Pietism
summary: In England and New England, Puritans sought a further reformation of church and life according to scripture, producing a rich literature of sermons, diaries and allegory. In Lutheran Germany, Pietists such as Spener and Francke emphasised conversion, small-group Bible study and practical charity over doctrinal controversy. Both movements prepared the way for the evangelical revivals.

name: Evangelical revivals
summary: Field preaching, hymn singing and a stress on personal conversion swept Britain and North America in the Great Awakening and the Methodist movement led by John and Charles Wesley and George Whitefield. Jonathan Edwards gave the revivals a theologian. In the same period Hasidism arose among eastern European Jews, and Jewish thinkers such as Moses Mendelssohn engaged the Enlightenment.

name: 19th-century theology
summary: Faced with Enlightenment criticism, historical scholarship of the Bible and modern science, theologians reworked religion around feeling, history and ethics. Schleiermacher founded liberal Protestant theology, Kierkegaard insisted on individual faith, and Newman moved from Anglicanism to Rome. Judaism divided into Reform, Orthodox and other movements, and new missionary and social movements multiplied.

name: 20th-century theology & ecumenism
summary: Two world wars and the Holocaust prompted searching theology: Barth's dialectical theology, Bonhoeffer's resistance writings, Tillich's existential theology and Buber's philosophy of dialogue. The ecumenical movement brought churches together in the World Council of Churches (1948), and the Second Vatican Council (1962–65) reshaped Catholicism. Religion also drove movements for social justice, most visibly the American civil rights movement.
